chapter_title: The Case of the Fifth Word (Mystery and Magic)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 11 periods = 495 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 8h 15min

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Cracking the Code: First Encounter with Encyclopedia Brown

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.101): pre-reading warm-up — match multiple meanings of 'case'.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick class conversation: what does the word 'case' mean to you? Invite three or four responses before revealing that the text uses the word in a surprising way.

Teacher reads aloud the opening pages of the story (p.101–106), pausing at key moments — Leroy's nickname, Chief Brown's troubled expression — to let students absorb the atmosphere before any formal questioning begins.

Students work in pairs on the 'Match the meanings of case' task from 'Let us read' (p.101), matching each sentence to its correct sense of the word. Teacher circulates and prompts where pairs are uncertain.
Whole-class share-out: pairs report their matches, and teacher builds a brief discussion on how context determines word meaning, drawing examples directly from the story's opening.

periods.teacher_notes: The opening of the story establishes the Browns' dinner-table ritual and Leroy's remarkable but quietly kept talent — draw students' attention to Chief Brown's body language as a signal that something unusual has occurred. A common pitfall is rushing the word-meaning matching without tying each sense back to a sentence context; insist students read each sentence aloud before choosing. Students who finish quickly may note other words in the opening pages that carry more than one meaning.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Inside the Case: Comprehension and Character

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.104): complete sentence starters with reasons about Leroy and Chief Brown.
Let us discuss (p.108): match textual evidence to Leroy's character traits.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.107): identify which statements about the story are facts and which are opinions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the two paragraphs (p.104) describing the Tuesday dinner scene aloud to refresh the class on the details they need for today's tasks.

Students individually complete the sentence-completion task from 'Let us discuss' (p.104) — four sentence starters about Leroy's nickname, Chief Brown's behaviour, Encyclopedia's silence, and Nolan's will. Teacher invites responses and asks the class to evaluate each reason given.

Students work with the character-traits matching table from 'Let us discuss' (p.108), pairing each piece of textual evidence with the trait it demonstrates. Teacher guides a whole-class discussion, asking students to justify each match with a line from the text.

Teacher poses the open question: 'Would Chief Brown have solved this case without Leroy?' Students share brief verbal responses; no written record is required, but teacher captures two contrasting views on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the dinner-table scene, students should be able to explain Leroy's nickname through the story's own evidence rather than general knowledge — push them to cite specific lines. A common pitfall on the character-traits table is selecting 'gentle' for evidence that actually points to 'humble'; guide students to weigh the trait against the textual action precisely. The fact-and-opinion classification task is set for independent follow-up at home.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Reading the Extracts: Inference and Close Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.109): extract 1 — Chief Brown's dilemma, Encyclopedia's motive, parents' naming choice.
Let us think and reflect (p.109–110): extract 2 — Chief Brown's reaction, Mrs. Brown's decoding attempt, coded message purpose.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 (p.109) aloud with expression, then invites students to paraphrase in one sentence what dilemma Chief Brown faces in those lines.

Students work through the four questions on Extract 1 from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.109) — sentence completion, two multiple-choice items, and a short-answer on the phrase 'stuck with'. Teacher leads a structured class discussion after each question, probing students to explain their reasoning.

Teacher reads Extract 2 (p.109–110) aloud; students then work on the four questions for that extract from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.109–110), focusing on Chief Brown's head-shake, Mrs. Brown's analysis, and the purpose of Encyclopedia's final reminder.

Whole-class synthesis: teacher asks students to identify the single most important inference they made across both extracts and justify it aloud; two or three students share, and the class briefly evaluates each justification.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the dinner-table scene and character traits, students are now ready to move from factual recall to inference — the extracts demand that they read between the lines rather than locate answers directly. A common pitfall is treating the MCQ on Encyclopedia's motive as a recall question; remind students the text does not state the reason directly, so they must infer from his behaviour across the story. Students who want to explore the coded message further may re-read the paragraph where Leroy reveals the day-of-the-week pattern on p.110–111 as self-study.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Beyond the Surface: Extended Response and Story Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.110): answer questions on Nolan–Davenport relationship, Mrs. Brown, Chief Brown's pride, and the coded message.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the story's resolution — the fir tree, the jug, the hidden jewellery — to anchor the class before they attempt the extended questions that require the whole-story arc.

Students work individually on the extended questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.110): textual evidence for Nolan and Davenport's closeness, Chief Brown's pride in his son, and the role of the four-word coded message in the plot. Teacher circulates, prompting students to use specific events from the story rather than general impressions.

Selected students share their responses aloud; class evaluates whether each answer is supported by textual evidence. Teacher draws attention to how Leroy's single well-chosen question — about the fir tree — encapsulates his method, and invites students to connect this to what they noted about his character traits earlier.

periods.teacher_notes: Having analysed both extracts closely in the previous reading unit, students now bring those inference skills to longer evidence-based responses — the jump is from sentence-level quotation to paragraph-level argument. A common pitfall in ECR answers on the Nolan–Davenport relationship is asserting closeness without citing the specific story detail that they met in prison and planned together; ask students to point to the paragraph before they write. The character-sketch writing task listed in the textbook is set as a self-study extension for interested students at p.110.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Sharpening the Eye and Ear: Observation Skills Podcast

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.117): mark four statements true or false while listening to the observation-skills podcast.
Let us listen (p.117): fill in five blanks with exact words from the second listening of the podcast.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the listening task: tell students they will hear a podcast about improving observation skills — the same quality that makes Leroy a superb detective. Students preview the four true/false statements on p.117 silently.
Teacher reads the podcast transcript aloud at a measured pace (p.151). Students mark the four statements as true or false on their own. Teacher does not pause or repeat during this first listening.
Brief class check on the true/false answers: students call out verdicts; teacher confirms and asks for a one-sentence reason for any statement marked false.
Teacher reads the podcast aloud a second time, slightly more slowly. Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank sentences from 'Let us listen' (p.117), writing only the exact words they hear.

Pair check: students compare their fill-in answers with a partner, then the class agrees on the correct words together. Teacher highlights how precise listening — catching exact words — mirrors the precise pattern-recognition Leroy uses in the story.

periods.teacher_notes: The podcast transcript (p.151) lists five practical tips for improving observation — slow down, engage all senses, ask questions, take notes, practise mindfulness — and students must distinguish these from their own paraphrases when filling blanks. A common pitfall is students writing near-synonyms rather than the exact words from the podcast; remind them that the task specifies one to three exact words heard. The thematic bridge to Leroy's observational genius helps sustain engagement with what can otherwise feel like a standalone task.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Voices in the Room: Pronunciation and Mystery Group Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.117): practise pronunciation of story vocabulary and commonly mispronounced English words.
Let us speak (p.117): conduct a structured group discussion on 'The Interesting Aspects of a Mystery Story'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the pronunciation of 'jewellery', 'clerk', and 'dessert' using the phonetic guides provided (p.117), then leads the class through the extended list — January, pizza, Wednesday, buffet, and others — with choral repetition and individual cold-calling.

Students form groups of five or six. Teacher distributes roles: one moderator, the rest as speakers. Teacher displays the turn-taking and agreement/disagreement phrases on the board and reviews them quickly.

Groups conduct their discussions on 'The Interesting Aspects of a Mystery Story'. The moderator opens, manages turns using raised-hand signals, and summarises. Teacher circulates, noting how well speakers use the provided phrases and whether participation is equitable.

Each group's moderator delivers a one-minute summary to the class. Teacher offers brief whole-class feedback on language use — particularly the agreement and interruption phrases — without singling out individuals.

periods.teacher_notes: The story's wealth of genre conventions — the coded message, the dinner-table ritual, the reluctant genius — gives groups rich material for their discussion; if a group stalls, prompt them to think about what makes the coded message more satisfying than a straightforward confession. A common pitfall in group discussions at this level is one or two students dominating; the moderator role is designed to prevent this, so brief the moderators before the discussion begins that equal participation is their responsibility. Students who are hesitant to speak should be encouraged to use the 'I agree because…' phrase as a low-risk entry point.
materials: Turn-taking and discussion phrases displayed on board

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Reporting the Event: Writing an Exhibition Report

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.117): plan and draft a report on an inter-school art exhibition using the provided sample format.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the model report on the inter-school football tournament from the textbook aloud, pointing out each structural feature: title with byline, the what/who/when/where opening paragraph, sequenced body paragraphs with markers, and the prize-giving closing paragraph.

Class jointly brainstorms the specific details needed for the art exhibition report — exhibition name, school, date, artworks, judges, prize-winners — and teacher records key ideas on the board. Students decide which details they will use in their own reports.

Students draft their full reports independently, working through each paragraph in the order modelled. Teacher circulates, nudging students who stall at the opening paragraph to answer the four wh-questions first before writing a sentence.

Students swap reports with a partner for a quick peer read: the partner checks that all four structural components are present and marks any missing element. Students make one or two corrections before the unit closes; reports are complete and finished within these minutes.

periods.teacher_notes: The model report on the football tournament provides a clear blueprint; the key teaching move is helping students understand that a report's value lies in its factual precision and chronological order, not in dramatic language. A common pitfall is students writing a narrative retelling of the event rather than a factual report with clear format markers — point to the sample's paragraph structure and sequence words explicitly before drafting begins. Students who want to explore report writing further may read other examples of event reports in newspapers or school magazines as self-study.
materials: English textbook (p.117 and the model report sample)

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Words in Action: Phrasal Verbs, Homophones, and Word Puzzles

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.111): match phrasal verbs from the story to meanings, then fill blanks using them.
Let us learn (p.111–112): fill blanks with correct homophone pairs from the given word box.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.113): solve the visual word puzzles — infer the hidden phrase from each illustration.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'figure out' and 'got away with' on the board and asks students to recall where they encountered these in the story — this anchors the phrasal verbs in the narrative context before the formal matching task.

Students complete the phrasal verb matching task from 'Let us learn' (p.111), then fill the six blanks using the matched verbs. Teacher reviews each answer with the class, asking students to name the story moment that connects to each phrasal verb.

Teacher introduces the homophone task by writing 'week/weak' on the board and eliciting the difference in meaning and spelling. Students complete the five homophone-pair sentences from 'Let us learn' (p.111–112) independently, then pairs check each other's choices.

Whole-class review of two or three homophone answers where disagreement arose; teacher reinforces the strategy of reading the full sentence for meaning clues before selecting. The visual word-puzzle task is introduced briefly and set as take-home exploration.

periods.teacher_notes: The phrasal verbs in this unit — 'turned up', 'cooled down', 'figure out', 'got away with' — all appear in the story's plot, so returning to the narrative context is the most effective way to make meanings stick. A common pitfall with the homophone task is students relying on sound alone and not checking the grammatical role of the word in the sentence; model the sentence-grammar check with the 'brake/break' pair before students work independently. The visual word puzzles are set for take-home exploration and need not be collected.
materials: Dictionary (optional, as suggested in the task)

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Grammar in the Story: Conjunctions and Reported Speech

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.113): fill blanks with relative and subordinating conjunctions to complete a detective-story paragraph.
Let us learn (p.115): study rules for reported speech and transform interrogative sentences from direct to indirect speech.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes two sentences from the story on the board that use relative and subordinating conjunctions (e.g., 'who', 'where', 'because') and asks students to identify the conjunction and describe what relationship it creates between the clauses.

Students complete the cloze paragraph on detective stories from 'Let us learn' (p.113), choosing the correct conjunction from the box for each blank. Teacher reviews the answers as a class, asking students to read the completed paragraph aloud to feel how conjunctions link ideas.

Teacher explains the rules for transforming interrogative direct speech to indirect speech using the examples from 'Let us learn' (p.115), focusing on tense shifts, pronoun changes, and the removal of question marks. Students then complete the five transformation exercises.

Three or four students read their reported-speech transformations aloud; the class identifies any tense or pronoun error and corrects it together. Teacher closes by pointing to the story's own dialogue between Mrs. Brown and Leroy as a real context where reported speech would apply.

periods.teacher_notes: The conjunction paragraph in 'Let us learn' (p.113) is centred on detective stories, making it a natural bridge from the narrative students have been reading. A common pitfall with reported speech transformation is students forgetting to shift both the pronoun and the tense simultaneously — address this by writing the two-step rule visibly on the board before the transformation task begins. Students who want additional practice may rewrite any two lines of dialogue from the story itself in indirect speech as a self-study exercise.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Eyes Wide Open: Optical Illusions, Word Games, and the Library

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.117): observe and discuss optical illusions — what the eye sees versus what is actually there.
Let us explore (p.117): play 'Name the Mystery Object' — teams prepare and respond to three-hint clues.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.117): visit the library, find an encyclopedia, and note how it differs from a dictionary.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the optical illusion images from 'Let us explore' (p.117) and invites students to describe what they see first, then what they see on looking again. Class discussion: how does this experience connect to the idea of observation and interpretation that runs through the story?

Teacher explains the rules of 'Name the Mystery Object' from 'Let us explore' (p.117) and uses the blackboard example to demonstrate the three-hint, points-decreasing format. Teams are formed and each team chooses and discusses their secret object quietly.

Teams take turns delivering their three hints while the opposing teams guess after each hint. Teacher keeps score on the board and ensures each team has at least one turn. If a team guesses correctly on the first hint, the guessing team earns the full twenty points.

Teacher introduces the library task from 'Let us explore' (p.117) as a take-home activity: students are asked to locate an encyclopedia on their next library visit and prepare one observation about how it differs from a dictionary to share when they return.

periods.teacher_notes: The optical illusion activity works best when students are encouraged to describe what they see with their own words before any explanation is offered — resist telling them what the 'correct' interpretation is too quickly. A common pitfall in the word game is teams preparing hints that are too easy or so cryptic that no one can guess; coach teams during their preparation minute that hints should be fair but challenging. The library visit task is set for independent follow-up and need not be collected formally.
materials: English textbook (p.117 — optical illusion images and word-game rules)

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: The Fifth Word Revisited: A Whole-Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses a single organising question on the board: 'What made Leroy's mind different from every other mind in this story?' Students spend a quiet few minutes jotting notes drawing on anything from the story — the coded message, his one targeted question, his deliberate ordinariness.

Whole-class discussion: students share their notes and the teacher builds a mind-map on the board connecting the strands — pattern recognition, lateral thinking, modesty, the dinner-table ritual — to show how the chapter's themes are woven together across the story.

Language play synthesis: teacher introduces two or three fresh wordplay puzzles in the spirit of the coded-days-of-the-week riddle — for example, short spoonerisms or a new 'remove three letters to find a hidden word' challenge — and pairs work to crack them, experiencing the same kind of lateral thinking Leroy demonstrated.

Each student writes a single paragraph — begun and completed in these minutes — answering: 'If you were to write the next Encyclopedia Brown case, what one clue would you hide in plain sight, and how?' The paragraph is a creative response grounded in the chapter's logic, not a continuation of any earlier draft.

Two or three volunteers read their paragraphs aloud. Teacher closes by noting that the chapter's real case is not just the jewellery theft — it is a case for the value of curiosity, careful observation, and quiet confidence in one's own thinking.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the full arc of the chapter — the story's plot, Leroy's character, the coded message, the vocabulary of observation, and the grammar of reporting — so all of that content is available to students regardless of which path brought them to this sitting. A common pitfall in synthesis discussions is students summarising the plot rather than reflecting on the ideas; redirect by returning to the organising question about what made Leroy's thinking distinctive. The creative writing paragraph is designed to begin and finish within the available minutes — keep it to one focused paragraph so every student completes it.
materials: English textbook (p.101–117, any page students wish to revisit)

items.item_stem: In 'The Case of the Fifth Word', Chief Brown searches Nolan's nursery with his officers and finds nothing. Which of the following statements correctly explains why the search failed?

options.label: A
options.text: Davenport had already collected the jewellery before the officers arrived at the nursery.

options.label: B
options.text: Nolan had moved the jewellery to a different location after his stroke.

options.label: C
options.text: The officers did not have a search warrant and were forced to leave early.

options.label: D
options.text: The stolen jewellery was hidden inside a twenty-gallon jug of earth beneath a young fir tree, an object officers would not think to uproot.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests a procedural misreading; the story does not mention a warrant issue.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads the plot — Davenport had disappeared and did not know the hiding place without the coded note.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a plot detail not present; Nolan dies before any relocation could occur.

items.source_lo: Student reads a prose narrative to locate explicit information, infer character motivation, and evaluate textual evidence using prose fiction as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Encyclopedia Brown, Chief Brown's dinner-table case, Nolan's coded four-word message, Leroy's character traits, and extract-based inference questions.
items.item_stem: Both Chief Brown and Mrs. Brown attempt to decode 'Nom Utes Sweden Hurts' but neither succeeds, while Leroy cracks the code with a single targeted question. What does the contrast between the adults' approach and Leroy's approach reveal about the kind of thinking the coded message requires? Support your answer with specific details from the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The adults look for the literal meaning of each word — Mrs. Brown identifies 'Nom' as short for 'nominative', 'Utes' as an American Indian tribe, and so on — while Leroy looks for a hidden pattern by stripping the letters 'd-a-y' from each word to reveal days of the week. This shows that the code requires lateral thinking and pattern recognition rather than knowledge of individual word meanings.

items.item_stem: Listen carefully to the podcast about improving observation skills. Read each statement below and write True or False based on what the podcast says.

options.text: Curious people tend to be better observers because they actively seek to understand what they notice.
Making sketches of a place weakens your memory of its features.
Observation involves only the sense of sight, not any other sense.
Slowing down and focusing on what is in front of you makes details clearer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — The podcast states observation involves hearing, smelling, touching, and even tasting, not sight alone.
2. True — The podcast says when you pause and observe, details become clearer.
3. True — The podcast states curious people tend to be better observers because they actively try to understand what they notice.
4. False — The podcast says making sketches strengthens understanding of a place's features.

Uses each chosen word in a grammatically complete sentence.
Sentence connects clearly to a story event or character.

items.item_stem: In a group of five, hold a discussion on this topic: 'The best mystery stories make readers feel they could have solved the puzzle themselves. Do you agree?' One student acts as the moderator. Use the polite turn-taking phrases you have practised, allow each member one uninterrupted turn, and have the moderator summarise the group's view at the end.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion with at least one reason from the story.
Uses a polite agreement or disagreement phrase at least once.
Listens without interrupting another speaker's turn.
Moderator's summary reflects the range of views expressed.

items.item_stem: Your school's Science Club recently organised an inter-school science quiz. Write a short report of four paragraphs following this plan: (1) title with your name as reporter; (2) an opening paragraph answering what, who, when, and where; (3) a paragraph describing two or three highlights of the event using sequence markers; (4) a closing paragraph on the prize-giving and any remarks made.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Leroy's classmate and you attended his school's annual talent show. Write a newspaper report of the event. Your report should go beyond simply listing facts — describe the atmosphere, quote one imagined remark from a participant or judge, and offer a closing sentence that reflects on why such events matter for the school community.

expected_elements: Uses formal report structure: title, byline, four paragraphs.
Includes descriptive language that conveys atmosphere.
Integrates one plausible direct quotation from a participant or judge.
Closing sentence reflects meaningfully on the event's value.

items.item_stem: Match each phrasal verb in Column A with its meaning in Column B. All six phrasal verbs appear in the story of Encyclopedia Brown.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A|Column B
figure out|(i) to wear (clothing or an accessory)
cooled down|(ii) to escape without being punished
turned up|(iii) to work out the answer to a problem
put on|(iv) to have an understanding or impression of something
got away with|(v) to appear or be discovered
make of|(vi) to become calm after excitement or anger

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: figure out – (iii); cooled down – (vi); turned up – (v); put on – (i); got away with – (ii); make of – (iv)

answer_key.right: (iii) to work out the answer to a problem
(vi) to become calm after excitement or anger
(iv) to have an understanding or impression of something

items.item_stem: Mrs. Brown says to Leroy, 'Can you figure out what these four words mean?' Rewrite this sentence in indirect speech, beginning with: Mrs. Brown asked Leroy ___. Then write one original sentence of your own using any other phrasal verb from the story (cooled down, turned up, got away with, or put on) to describe an imagined moment in the lives of the Brown family.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Mrs. Brown asked Leroy if he could figure out what those four words meant. (Accept any original sentence correctly using one of the listed phrasal verbs in a plausible Brown-family context, with correct tense and subject.)

items.item_stem:
In the 'Name the Mystery Object' game, teams give three hints in order from hardest to easiest — the first hint earns the most points. Below is a set of three hints for a mystery object connected to the world of Leroy Brown. Read the hints and write the name of the object. Then explain, in one sentence, why the hints are arranged from hardest to easiest rather than easiest to hardest.

Hint 1 (20 points): I store information on every subject, organised alphabetically.
Hint 2 (10 points): Leroy's friends compared him to me and called him more user-friendly.
Hint 3 (5 points): My name is also Leroy's nickname.

expected_elements: Correctly identifies the mystery object as an encyclopedia.
Explains that harder hints first rewards sharper observation and reasoning.
Links the game's scoring logic to the story's theme of careful thinking.
Uses at least one specific detail from the hints or the story.

items.item_stem: Design your own 'Name the Mystery Object' game card for a classmate. Choose an object, person, or place from the story of Leroy Brown — or from the world of observation and investigation the story explores. Write three hints in the correct order (most challenging first, easiest last), assign the correct point values (20, 10, 5), and explain in two sentences what skill of observation or thinking a player needs in order to crack your puzzle on the very first hint.

expected_elements: Game card has three hints in descending difficulty with correct point values.
Hints are specific, fair, and clearly connected to the chosen subject.
Object, person, or place is drawn from the story's world.
Explanation names the observational or reasoning skill required for Hint 1.
